title: IES Profiles: From File Rows to Runtime Sampling
abstract: This article explains the structure of an IES file, how Unreal Engine imports it, and how to store its data in a custom texture for sampling.
image: /content/blog/IES Profiles - From File Rows to Runtime Sampling/ies-file-anatomy.svg
imageAlt: An IES file parsed into directional intensity in candela and stored in a texture
lede: An IES file is a measured table of luminous intensity by direction. Unreal Engine can import it to create richer light distributions. However, Unreal normalizes the data to simplify its calculations, so the texture alone does not provide exact directional intensity in candela. This implementation converts the IES data into a texture that runtime code can sample directly for absolute directional intensity.

sections.heading: What an IES file describes
paragraphs: An IES file is a text file based on the IES LM-63 standard. Luminaire manufacturers and test laboratories use it to record the luminous intensity emitted by a fixture in each measured direction. In simple terms, it is a table of intensity in candela indexed by vertical angle θ and horizontal angle φ.
Lighting artists commonly use these files to reproduce real fixtures in a renderer. In Unreal Engine, an imported IES profile can be assigned to Point and Rect Lights to change the shape of the beam.

equations.label: Directional intensity from IES data
equations.expression: I_abs(θ, φ) = I_IES(θ, φ) × M_cd × F_ballast
terms: F_ballast is the Ballast Factor, a lumen factor that represents energy loss.
Lumens per Lamp is the total visible light output of one lamp within the luminaire; it is not used in this calculation.

rows: The LM-63 revision, manufacturer, and summary information about the luminaire.

Lamps: number of light sources; Lumens per Lamp: total visible light output of one lamp; Candela Multiplier; verticalCount and horizontalCount: numbers of measured vertical and horizontal angles; photometricType: distribution type; unitType: units; and width, length, and height: dimensions of the luminous area.
Ballast Factor, futureUse reserved data, and input watts.
An array of vertical measurement angles with the count given above, usually covering 0°–180°. The reverse side is covered by the horizontal-angle records through 360°.
An array of horizontal measurement angles with the count given above, generally covering 0°–360°.
The measured directional-intensity table: rows represent horizontal records and columns represent vertical records.

callouts.title: Scope
callouts.text: This implementation targets the LM-63-2002 revision.

sections.heading: How Unreal Engine imports it
paragraphs: Unreal Engine imports an IES file as a UTextureLightProfile, which derives from UTexture2D. During import, it parses the angle arrays, reconstructs the symmetry recorded in the file, and resamples the distribution into a texture.

Unreal stores the imported data in a normalized 0–1 texture. In other words, the texture keeps only the shape of the distribution; the directional intensity is approximated using Brightness and Texture Multiplier.

rows: Maximum directional-intensity value obtained during import.
Scale associated with normalization. Its exact role was unclear from the source; the default appears to be 1.0f.
Chooses between Brightness and the Intensity set in the Editor.

callouts.title: Limitation
callouts.text: Unreal does not account for Ballast Factor, and Brightness records only the maximum directional-intensity value. Therefore, Brightness × Texture Multiplier × IES Texture Sample cannot be relied on to recover exact directional intensity.

sections.heading: Create an absolute-cd texture
paragraphs: The horizontal axis represents vertical angle θ from 0° to 180°, and the vertical axis represents horizontal angle φ from 0° to 360°.
For each texel, calculate the horizontal and vertical angles, then find and interpolate the four surrounding directional-intensity samples in candela.

equations.label: Texture UV
terms: Each texel stores T(u, v) = I_abs(θ, φ) in cd.

equations.label: Interpolation weights
equations.expression: tθ = (θ − θ₀) / (θ₁ − θ₀),  tφ = (φ − φ₀) / (φ₁ − φ₀)
terms: θ₀, θ₁ and φ₀, φ₁ are the measured angles surrounding the target direction.

equations.label: Bilinear interpolation
equations.expression: I(θ, φ) = (1 − tφ)[(1 − tθ)I₀₀ + tθI₁₀] + tφ[(1 − tθ)I₀₁ + tθI₁₁]
terms: I₀₀, I₁₀, I₀₁, and I₁₁ are the four surrounding directional-intensity samples in candela.

sections.heading: Sample at runtime
paragraphs: Using the viewpoint as an example, first calculate the normalized direction from the light to the camera. Then map the vertical and horizontal angles to UV coordinates.

equations.label: Normalized light-to-camera direction
terms: d is the normalized direction from the light to the camera.

equations.label: Vertical angle
equations.expression:
θ = arccos(clamp(F · d, −1, 1))
u = θ / π
terms: F is the light's normalized forward direction.

equations.label: Horizontal angle
equations.expression:
C₀ = −U,  C₉₀ = −R
φ = atan2(d · C₉₀, d · C₀),  v = mod(φ + 2π, 2π) / 2π
terms: U is the light's normalized up direction.
R is the light's normalized right direction.
If the result is reversed, adjust the signs to match the implementation's orientation convention.

equations.label: Directional intensity in candela
terms: Because T stores absolute values, I_dir is in cd.

sections.heading: Convert cd to cd/m² using the light-source area
paragraphs: Luminance in cd/m² is directional intensity in cd per square metre. For a flat light source with uniform luminance, calculating the luminance received from a direction requires the projected area and the viewing angle.

technicalTables.caption: w and h are the half-width and half-height in cm, matching Unreal Engine's internal unit; r is the radius; 10⁻⁴ converts cm² to m².

callouts.title: Current photometric calculation
callouts.text: Because the implementation samples absolute IES candela directly, it no longer uses Unreal Engine's Intensity or Brightness.
